sections.h2: What sets a St. Petersburg sale apart
sections.html:
Waterfront location, storm repairs and permit history decide how fast a St. Petersburg house closes. The city sits on a peninsula in Pinellas County, with 244 miles of shoreline along Tampa Bay, Boca Ciega Bay, the Gulf of Mexico and intracoastal waterways. More than 265,000 people live here, spread over 100-plus neighborhoods.

The coast supports prices and complicates disclosure. Buyers, lenders and insurers ask whether the property is in a flood hazard area, whether past storm damage was repaired under permit, and what the city has on file. Proximity to the waterfront, the Pier and downtown can move prices block by block, so compare your house with sales in your own neighborhood. Collect your answers early and you can accept a strong offer quickly, whether it comes from a listing or a cash buyer.

sections.h2: Permit history and the building department
sections.html:
Permit and flood records sit with the city's Construction Services and Permitting Division at the Municipal Services Center, One 4th St. N. Homeowners are expected to get permits before repair, improvement or construction begins.

Florida House Bill 803 lets the city issue a Permit Exemption form for work on a single-family dwelling totaling less than $7,500. It applies only outside flood hazard areas and does not cover structural components (window, door, roofing, soffit and siding work), mechanical, electrical, plumbing or gas work.

Certificates issued by the St. Petersburg permitting office
CertificateWhen it is needed
Certificate of OccupancyNew construction, change of use, combining units, rebuilding after condemnation or fire
Temporary Certificate of OccupancyNew construction delayed on a non life-safety item, once major trades have a partial final
Certificate of CompletionFinished work that does not need a CO; required for a building shell, otherwise optional
Elevation CertificateFEMA document showing height above sea level and base flood elevation; city records go back to 1990

You can research Certificate of Occupancy history for free in the city's property cards database. Pull yours before you list. If you visit in person, bring a photo ID and a floor layout. An optional preliminary plan review is also available, handy if a buyer wants to add to the house after closing.

If your house is in a flood hazard area and was damaged, the repair path matters to the sale. The permitting office points owners to FEMA's 49% Rule, which can affect a property after storm damage, and asks visitors to bring photos, a damage summary and a floor layout.

There is a tax side too. When a structure is damaged or destroyed, taxes can still rise for long-time homesteaded owners because of the Save Our Homes cap recapture rule, and if the building value fell below land value, the assessed value may not drop. Read any value reconsideration letters you receive, since a building value can differ from the year before.

  • Keep storm photos, adjuster reports and repair invoices together.
  • Find out whether the city holds an elevation certificate for your address.
  • Confirm every repair that needed a permit has a final inspection.
  • Ask the buyer's insurer early about flood coverage, since it can change the closing timeline.

Cash buyers often purchase storm-damaged houses as they are, but expect a discount tied to the unknowns.

sections.h2: Pinellas County property taxes at a sale
sections.html:
Your home's value is set as of January 1 by the Pinellas County Property Appraiser, and the bill arrives from the Pinellas County Tax Collector in November. After you sell, the county removes the exemptions and caps you had on the next January 1, and the new owner's value moves toward market.

The homestead exemption, worth up to $50,000 of taxable value, needs an application by March 1. Paying early earns 4 percent off in November, shrinking to 1 percent by February. At closing, the agent prorates the year's taxes between you and the buyer.

A buyer coming from another Florida homestead may carry over a savings cap through portability. The buyer files that application, within three years of January 1 of the year the earlier homestead was given up.

Documentary stamp tax on a Pinellas deed runs 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and the clerk takes it when the deed is recorded. Every party on the document stays liable under Department of Revenue rules, even if the contract puts the cost on one side.

Statute 28.24 sets recording at $5.00 for page one and $4.00 for each added page, with further per-page charges on top. The settlement statement lists each item.

Cash offers often skip lender steps such as appraisals, which can shorten the schedule. Even so, ask who covers title insurance, stamp tax and tax proration, and get the split in writing before you accept.

Before hiring anyone, confirm the contractor's license through the Pinellas County Licensing Board. Trouble scheduling an inspection can trace back to an unknown license status, so permits and licenses are tied closely here.

For work in progress, the city's online portal lets you enter a permit number to schedule or cancel an inspection and to check plan review status trade by trade. E-plan applicants have ten business days to finish uploads or answer comments before the application is denied and the workflow ends.

  • Look up each contractor on the county licensing board's site.
  • Enter permit numbers in the city portal to see open reviews.
  • Call the permitting division at 727-893-7231 with license status questions.

A buyer's inspector will usually find stalled work, so finish it first or disclose it.

A listing means preparing the house, opening it for showings and answering repair requests after the buyer's inspection. The price can be higher, and the timeline is longer. With a cash buyer, you usually sell as-is, and the date depends on title work instead of a lender.

Before you commit to either, ask each buyer or agent how they would treat open permits and storm damage, because that answer shapes the price. Whichever route you choose, the steps are the same at the end: the title agent searches the records, any liens and mortgages are paid from proceeds, you sign the deed, and the clerk records it. Gather the deed, permit list, storm records and a recent tax bill beforehand, and you can answer an offer in days instead of weeks. If the house is vacant, arrange for someone to check it after storms, keep utilities on until closing, and hand over every key at the table.

faqs.q: Where do I get permit records for a St. Petersburg house?
faqs.a: Ask the city's Construction Services and Permitting Division at One 4th St. N. A free property cards database covers Certificate of Occupancy history, and the online portal tracks permit status.

faqs.q: Do small repairs in St. Petersburg need a permit?
faqs.a: Not always. A form lets the city exempt single-family work under $7,500 outside flood hazard areas, but not structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing or gas work. Check with the building department first.

faqs.q: Does the buyer get my Save Our Homes cap?
faqs.a: No. The assessment returns to just value on the next January 1 after a sale, so the buyer's bill may be much higher than yours. A new homestead exemption can be filed by the buyer through March 1.

faqs.q: Is selling a storm-damaged St. Petersburg house as is possible?
faqs.a: Yes. Plenty of buyers take houses as-is, though you should disclose known damage and any unpermitted repairs. In a flood hazard area, ask the city about FEMA's 49% Rule before you decide to repair or sell.

faqs.q: How do I check a contractor's license?
faqs.a: Use the Pinellas County Licensing Board's site. For permit questions tied to a license, call the permitting division at 727-893-7231.
